tips.title: Strong is not concentrated
tips.body: **Strong and weak** are about **how completely the acid ionises**. **Dilute and concentrated** are about **how much acid there is** in a given volume. They are independent: you can have a **concentrated weak** acid — bottled vinegar — and a **dilute strong** one.

tips.title: Three of each
tips.body: **Strong**: hydrochloric, nitric, sulfuric. **Weak**: ethanoic, citric, carbonic. The strong three are the laboratory acids; the weak three are the ones you meet in food and fizzy drinks.

tips.title: Each pH unit is a factor of ten
tips.body: Down **one** pH unit is **×10** the hydrogen ions. Down **three** is $10^3 = 1000$. Count the units, then raise ten to that power — and remember that going **up** the scale **divides**.

tips.title: Lower pH means more hydrogen ions
tips.body: The scale runs the opposite way to the thing it measures. **Low pH = high $\mathrm{H^+}$ concentration = more acidic.** If your answer has a higher pH with more hydrogen ions, you have it inverted.

tips.title: Weak acids are reversible
tips.body: A weak acid **partially** ionises, so the equation has a **reversible arrow**: $\mathrm{CH_3COOH \rightleftharpoons CH_3COO^- + H^+}$. A strong acid ionises **completely**, so its arrow goes one way only.

steps.title: What strong and weak mean
steps.body:
**This part of the specification is Higher tier only.**

**A strong acid is completely ionised in aqueous solution.** Every acid molecule splits into ions, releasing all of its hydrogen as $\mathrm{H^+}$ ions.

Examples: **hydrochloric, nitric and sulfuric** acids — the three laboratory acids.

**A weak acid is only partially ionised in aqueous solution.** Only a small fraction of the molecules split up at any moment; the rest stay as whole molecules.

Examples: **ethanoic, citric and carbonic** acids — vinegar, citrus fruit, and fizzy water.

**The difference is written in the arrow.** A strong acid ionises completely, so its ionisation goes one way:

$$\mathrm{HCl \rightarrow H^+ + Cl^-}$$

A weak acid only partially ionises, so its ionisation is **reversible** and sits in an equilibrium with most of the acid still as molecules:

$$\mathrm{CH_3COOH \rightleftharpoons CH_3COO^- + H^+}$$

**So for the same concentration of acid**, the strong acid puts **far more $\mathrm{H^+}$ ions** into the solution than the weak one does. That single fact explains everything else in this topic.

steps.title: Strong is not concentrated
steps.body:
**The specification asks you to use and explain four terms**, and they form two independent pairs:

- **Strong** and **weak** — about the **degree of ionisation**. Does the acid split into ions completely, or only partly?
- **Dilute** and **concentrated** — about the **amount of substance** in a given volume. How much acid is dissolved in the water?

**These are independent**, which is exactly why questions are set on them. All four combinations exist:

- **Concentrated strong** — the hydrochloric acid in a stockroom bottle
- **Dilute strong** — the hydrochloric acid you use in class
- **Concentrated weak** — vinegar, which is largely ethanoic acid
- **Dilute weak** — the same vinegar with water added

**So a concentrated weak acid can have a higher pH than a dilute strong one.** There is a lot of ethanoic acid in the vinegar, but very little of it is ionised at any moment; there is little hydrochloric acid in the dilute solution, but **all** of it is ionised. What the pH responds to is the **concentration of $\mathrm{H^+}$ ions**, not the concentration of acid.

**Getting this the wrong way round is the commonest error in the topic.** Saying *sulfuric acid is strong because it is concentrated* uses one word to define the other, and earns nothing.

steps.title: pH and hydrogen ion concentration
steps.body:
**For a given concentration of aqueous solutions, the stronger an acid, the lower the pH.** More ionisation means more $\mathrm{H^+}$ ions, and more $\mathrm{H^+}$ ions means a lower pH.

**And the scale is not linear.** As the **pH decreases by one unit, the hydrogen ion concentration increases by a factor of 10.**

$$\text{factor} = 10^{\text{number of pH units}}$$

So a change of three pH units is a factor of $10^3 = 1000$, not three. Questions on this are **order of magnitude** calculations, and the answer is always a power of ten.

steps.title: What you would actually see
steps.body:
**Strength is not directly visible, so questions give you evidence and ask you to infer it.** Two kinds of evidence appear.

**pH, at equal concentration.** Put hydrochloric acid and ethanoic acid side by side at the **same concentration** and measure both. The hydrochloric acid has the **lower pH**, because it is **completely ionised** and so has a **higher $\mathrm{H^+}$ concentration**.

**Rate of reaction, at equal concentration.** Add magnesium to each. The **strong** acid fizzes **faster**, because the **higher concentration of $\mathrm{H^+}$ ions** means more frequent collisions with the metal. Both eventually produce the **same volume of hydrogen** if the same amount of acid was used — the weak acid is slower, not smaller.

**That last point is worth holding on to.** A weak acid is **not** a lesser acid in total. As its $\mathrm{H^+}$ ions are used up, more molecules ionise to replace them, so in the end the same quantity of acid reacts. The difference is **rate**, not amount.

**The phrase that makes these comparisons valid** is *at the same concentration*. Without it, nothing can be concluded: a concentrated weak acid may well have a lower pH than a dilute strong one. A question that omits the phrase is usually testing whether you noticed.

steps.title: Going deeper
steps.body:
**Define strength by ionisation, never by concentration.** A strong acid is **completely ionised**; a weak acid is **partially ionised**. The moment an answer reaches for *how much acid there is*, it has answered the wrong question. The clean test: *strong* and *weak* describe the **molecules**, *dilute* and *concentrated* describe the **solution**.

**The arrow carries the definition.** $\mathrm{HCl \rightarrow H^+ + Cl^-}$ goes one way, because none of it stays as molecules. $\mathrm{CH_3COOH \rightleftharpoons CH_3COO^- + H^+}$ is **reversible**, because most of it does. Drawing the right arrow is a compact way of showing you understand the difference.

**pH responds to $\mathrm{H^+}$ concentration, not to acid concentration.** This is what makes a **concentrated weak** acid possible: plenty of acid, very little of it ionised. So a comparison of pH only tells you about strength when the two solutions are at the **same concentration** — and a question that omits that phrase is usually testing whether you noticed.

**The scale is logarithmic, so answer in powers of ten.** One pH unit is **×10**, so a fall of 4 units is $10^4 = 10000$. Multiplying by the number of units instead of raising ten to it is the standard arithmetic slip, and it produces an answer far too small.

**Rate differs; total amount does not.** Given equal amounts at equal concentration, the strong acid reacts **faster** because it has more $\mathrm{H^+}$ ions at any moment. But the weak acid **keeps ionising** as its ions are consumed, so the **same total** quantity reacts and the **same volume of hydrogen** is collected. Answers that say the weak acid produces less have mistaken a rate for a yield.

**And the direction of the scale is a free check.** Lower pH always means **more** hydrogen ions and a **more acidic** solution. If a conclusion has the higher pH being more acidic, the scale has been read backwards.

steps.title: Summary
steps.body:
- **This spec point is Higher tier only.**
- A **strong acid is completely ionised** in aqueous solution: **hydrochloric, nitric, sulfuric**.
- A **weak acid is only partially ionised**: **ethanoic, citric, carbonic**.
- Strong acid ionisation is **one way**: $\mathrm{HCl \rightarrow H^+ + Cl^-}$.
- Weak acid ionisation is **reversible**: $\mathrm{CH_3COOH \rightleftharpoons CH_3COO^- + H^+}$.
- **Strong and weak** are about **degree of ionisation**; **dilute and concentrated** are about **amount of substance**.
- The two are **independent** — a **concentrated weak** acid and a **dilute strong** acid both exist.
- **For a given concentration, the stronger the acid, the lower the pH.**
- pH responds to the concentration of **$\mathrm{H^+}$ ions**, not of acid.
- **As pH decreases by one unit, the hydrogen ion concentration increases by a factor of 10.**
- So a fall of $n$ pH units is a factor of $10^n$.
- At the **same concentration**, a strong acid reacts **faster** with a metal, because there are more $\mathrm{H^+}$ ions.
- But the **same total volume of hydrogen** is produced, because the weak acid **keeps ionising** as it reacts.
- A strong acid also has a **higher electrical conductivity**, because there are more ions.
- **Lower pH always means more hydrogen ions** — a free check on any conclusion.

questions.prompt: Explain the difference between a strong acid and a concentrated acid, and describe two experiments that would distinguish a strong acid from a weak acid of the same concentration.
questions.solution:
**Strong** and **concentrated** describe two different things, and the fact that they are often confused is why the specification asks for both.

**Strength** is about **degree of ionisation**. A **strong acid is completely ionised** in aqueous solution — every molecule splits, releasing all of its hydrogen as $\mathrm{H^+}$ ions, as in $\mathrm{HCl \rightarrow H^+ + Cl^-}$. A **weak acid is only partially ionised**; most of it stays as whole molecules, and its ionisation is written with a **reversible** arrow, as in $\mathrm{CH_3COOH \rightleftharpoons CH_3COO^- + H^+}$.

**Concentration** is about **amount of substance** in a given volume — how much acid is dissolved in the water. It says nothing about whether that acid ionises.

Because the two are **independent**, all four combinations exist. Bottled vinegar is a **concentrated weak** acid; the hydrochloric acid used in a classroom is a **dilute strong** one. It follows that a concentrated weak acid can have a **higher pH** than a dilute strong acid, because pH responds to the concentration of **hydrogen ions**, not of acid.

Two experiments would distinguish them, and both require the acids to be **at the same concentration** — otherwise any difference could be caused by concentration rather than strength.

First, **measure the pH** of each with a pH probe. The **strong acid gives the lower pH**, because complete ionisation gives a **higher $\mathrm{H^+}$ concentration**. The difference is larger than it looks: three pH units is a factor of $10^3 = 1000$ in hydrogen ion concentration.

Second, **add magnesium ribbon** to equal volumes of each and compare the **rate of fizzing**. The strong acid reacts **faster**, because more $\mathrm{H^+}$ ions are present at any moment, so collisions with the metal are more frequent. What is worth noting is that the **total volume of hydrogen collected is the same**: as the weak acid's ions are consumed, **more molecules ionise** to replace them, so the same amount of acid reacts in the end. The difference between the two acids is one of **rate**, not of amount. Measuring **electrical conductivity** would work equally well, and for the same reason: the strong acid contains **more ions** to carry the current.

questions.prompt: The pH of a solution changes from 6 to 2. Explain what this tells you about the hydrogen ion concentration, and why the pH scale is defined in this way rather than as a simple count of ions.
questions.solution:
The rule is that **as the pH decreases by one unit, the hydrogen ion concentration increases by a factor of 10**. The scale is therefore a scale of **powers of ten**, not a simple count.

Here the pH falls from **6 to 2**, which is a change of **four** pH units. The factor is therefore $10^4 = \mathbf{10\,000}$: the solution now contains **ten thousand times** as many hydrogen ions per unit volume as it did. It is worth being deliberate about this, because the commonest error is to treat the change as a factor of **four** — multiplying by the number of units instead of raising ten to it — which understates the answer by more than three orders of magnitude.

The reason the scale is defined this way is that **hydrogen ion concentrations span an enormous range**. Between a strong laboratory acid and a strong alkali the concentration varies by something like a factor of $10^{14}$. Written out as ordinary numbers those values would be unwieldy — long strings of zeros or tiny decimals — and almost impossible to compare at a glance. Compressing them into a scale that runs from **0 to 14** makes them manageable, and it means a difference that matters chemically shows up as a difference of one or two units rather than of several zeros.

The cost of that convenience is that the scale is **not linear**, and it is easy to underestimate differences. A solution at pH 2 is not three times more acidic than one at pH 5; it is **a thousand times** more acidic.

Finally, the **direction** of the scale is worth stating explicitly, because it runs opposite to the quantity it describes: a **lower** pH means **more** hydrogen ions and a **more acidic** solution. That makes a useful free check on any conclusion — if an answer ends up with the higher pH being the more acidic solution, the scale has been read backwards.

examTechnique.body:
Two ideas and one calculation. The ideas are that **strength is degree of ionisation** and **concentration is amount of substance**, and that they are **independent**. The calculation is that each pH unit is a **factor of ten**.

Watch for the phrase **at the same concentration** in any comparison. Without it, a pH difference tells you nothing about strength, and questions omit it deliberately.
examinerErrors: Defining **strong** in terms of **concentrated**, or the reverse.
Saying a weak acid is one that has been **diluted**.
Treating a fall of $n$ pH units as a factor of $n$ rather than $10^n$.
Comparing the pH of two acids **without** fixing the concentration.
Saying a weak acid produces **less hydrogen** with a metal, when it produces the same amount more slowly.
Using a **single arrow** in the ionisation equation of a **weak** acid.
Reading the pH scale backwards, so a higher pH is treated as more acidic.
Forgetting that this spec point is **Higher tier only** and that the weak acid examples are **ethanoic, citric and carbonic**.
examTechnique.grade9Looks: A grade 9 answer keeps the two pairs of words apart without being prompted, and can produce the case that proves they are independent: a **concentrated weak** acid beside a **dilute strong** one. It writes the **reversible arrow** for a weak acid and says why. In calculation it answers in **powers of ten** and sanity-checks the direction — lower pH, more ions. And on the magnesium experiment it separates **rate** from **amount**: the strong acid is faster because more $\mathrm{H^+}$ ions are present at any moment, but the weak acid **keeps ionising**, so the same volume of hydrogen is collected in the end.
